name: Gonadoblastoma
aliases: in situ germ cell neoplasm of streak gonad

clinicalPearls: A tumour composed of both germ cells and sex cord-stromal elements that arises almost exclusively in dysgenetic gonads containing Y-chromosome material
Although the lesion itself is considered benign (an in situ germ cell neoplasm), it carries a substantial risk of progression to an invasive malignant germ cell tumour, most often a dysgerminoma
Classic at-risk settings include complete and partial gonadal dysgenesis with a 46,XY karyotype (Swyer syndrome), mixed gonadal dysgenesis, and Turner syndrome variants carrying Y-chromosome material
The malignant potential is linked to a locus on the Y chromosome (the gonadoblastoma-on-Y region containing TSPY)
The streak or dysgenetic gonad is typically non-functional, so patients often present with delayed puberty, primary amenorrhoea, or features of the underlying disorder of sex development
Because of the malignancy risk, prophylactic removal of dysgenetic Y-bearing gonads (gonadectomy) is recommended, with timing individualised to the specific diagnosis
Detection of Y-chromosome material on karyotype or molecular testing in a girl with gonadal dysgenesis is the key trigger for considering gonadectomy
reference.pathophysiology: Gonadoblastoma develops in gonads that have failed to differentiate normally (dysgenetic or streak gonads) when Y-chromosome material is present. Genes on the Y chromosome, particularly within the gonadoblastoma region that includes TSPY, are thought to promote survival and abnormal proliferation of germ cells within a disorganised stromal environment, producing a mixed germ-cell and sex cord-stromal lesion. The tumour is regarded as an in situ neoplasm, but the same germ cells can undergo malignant transformation to an invasive germ cell tumour such as dysgerminoma. The dysgenetic gonad itself produces little or no sex steroid, so affected individuals commonly show hypergonadotropic hypogonadism and the phenotype of their underlying disorder of sex development.
additionalDifferentials: Dysgerminoma or other malignant germ cell tumour of the gonad
Sex cord-stromal tumour of the ovary or testis
Streak gonad without tumour in gonadal dysgenesis
Ovarian germ cell tumour in a phenotypic female
Other causes of primary amenorrhoea and hypergonadotropic hypogonadism
Teratoma or mixed germ cell tumour
additionalInvestigations: Karyotype and molecular testing for Y-chromosome material in gonadal dysgenesis or disorder of sex development
Serum LH and FSH (typically elevated) with sex-steroid levels (low)
Germ cell tumour markers (for example lactate dehydrogenase, alpha-fetoprotein, and beta-hCG) to assess for malignant transformation
Pelvic and abdominal imaging to localise gonads and detect a mass
Histological examination of removed gonadal tissue to confirm the diagnosis and exclude invasive tumour
Assessment for the wider features of the underlying disorder of sex development
redFlags: Identification of Y-chromosome material in a patient with a dysgenetic or streak gonad, indicating malignancy risk and the need to consider gonadectomy
A rapidly enlarging pelvic or abdominal mass suggesting invasive germ cell malignancy
Signs of metastatic disease such as lymphadenopathy or systemic symptoms
reference.prognosis: When dysgenetic Y-bearing gonads are removed before malignant transformation, the outlook is excellent and the risk of invasive germ cell tumour is essentially eliminated; if an invasive tumour has already developed, prognosis depends on tumour type and stage, though dysgerminoma is generally chemosensitive with favourable outcomes.
pitfalls: Failing to karyotype patients with gonadal dysgenesis and therefore missing occult Y-chromosome material that mandates gonadectomy
Delaying prophylactic gonadectomy in a Y-bearing dysgenetic gonad and allowing malignant progression
Assuming a streak gonad carries no tumour risk irrespective of karyotype
Overlooking the diagnosis in a phenotypic female presenting only with primary amenorrhoea
Neglecting hormone replacement and the broader care needs of the underlying disorder of sex development after gonadectomy
management: Perform prophylactic bilateral gonadectomy of dysgenetic Y-bearing gonads to prevent malignant transformation, with timing individualised to the underlying diagnosis
Where an invasive germ cell tumour such as dysgerminoma has developed, treat with oncological surgery and platinum-based chemotherapy according to type and stage
Provide oestrogen and progestogen hormone replacement to induce and maintain puberty and protect bone health after gonadectomy
Identify at-risk individuals with karyotyping and molecular testing for Y-chromosome material in gonadal dysgenesis or disorder of sex development
Undertake surveillance with germ cell tumour markers (lactate dehydrogenase, alpha-fetoprotein, beta-hCG) and imaging where gonads are retained or before surgery
Coordinate multidisciplinary disorder-of-sex-development, endocrine, gynaecology and oncology care with psychological support and genetic counselling
